strengths: The paper tackles a well motivated and relevant topic: the links between GANs and score-based diffusion models, unifying both of them in a single framework, which is interesting as it opens up potentially fruitful areas of research.
The unifying equation DiffFlow and its dual interpretation between GANs and diffusion models is novel, providing a new non-conventional perspective on both models.
Some of the introduced algorithms, like Diffusion-GAN, are original as well.
To my understanding (up to mathematical details in the appendix that I could not thoroughly check), the theoretical derivations seem correct.
Finally, the derivations in the paper are, for the most part, clearly written (except Section 3.3).
The core ideas and intuitions of the paper are well presented, especially regarding the details of the particular cases of DiffFlow which are well articulated between each other.
The formulation and motivation of the unified SDE is clear.

The proposed DiffFlow formulation leads to a natural design of DiffFlow-GAN algorithm; based on the discussion provided by the authors in appendix C, this formulation also offers explanations and solutions on the instability of vanilla GAN training.
This work contains an extensive set of theoretical analysis to the SDE.
Originality: they proposed an object function that theoretically integrates GANs and SDMs.
Quality: written in detail so that even unfamiliar readers can understand.
Clarity: very well written and easy to read.
Significance: while there have been many studies attempting to integrate GANs and SDMs, theoretical explanations have been lacking, but this paper's theoretical part is very rich.

This paper provides an elegant unification of diffusion models and generative adversarial networks, which are two dominating methods for deep generative modelling, both of which are of great practical significance.
The unification is more than just a simple weighted combination as exemplified by the marginal preserving property.
Existing frameworks are demonstrated to be instantiations of this unification such as TDPM, VP SDE, DDPM etc., attesting to the generality of the claims made.
weaknesses: The paper suffers from strong overclaiming of its results; clarifying the claims and adjusting them so that they are properly supported by theoretical or empirical evidence is a necessity.
The unifying framework does exist, but there is no element supporting the rest of the claim in the paper.
The properties of the newly introduced algorithms are not assessed with any experiment.
There is no concrete discussion as to why the framework enables exact likelihood inference in its general case (and in particular, for GANs).

The unifying framework only encompasses derivations of the vanilla GAN model from Goodfellow et al. (2014), and not all GANs (like Wasserstein GANs); this should be explicitly stated, starting from the abstract.
The link of DiffFlow with GANs in Section 3.3 is loose and presented in an unclear fashion.

The development of Section 3.3 is incomplete to fully understand the presented contribution, as it misses details on how to handle the generator; the development in Appendix Section B should be moved into the main paper for completeness.
Even taking into account Appendix Section B, the link with GANs remains loose.

The paper establishes that the gradient of the log ratio corresponds to an optimal vanilla GAN discriminator, but how this can be articulated with GAN generators is left unfinished in the appendix; for example, Equations 27 and 28 only deal with the evolution of generator parameters w.r.t. training time and do not correspond to Equations 12 or 13 in the main paper, hence to DiffFlow.

Appendix Section K frames TPDM (Zheng et al., 2022) using the DiffFlow equation, but TPDM's first step is a forward pass through a generator, not a discriminator‑guided dynamics, which is not encompassed in the proposed framework.
The presentation lacks contextualization with already existing works, making the results appear more innovative than they actually are.
Proposition 1 is similar to results already obtained by Song et al. (2021) [3], who already needed to compute the variance of the marginal distributions.

The noise‑corrupting strategies for vanilla GANs mentioned in Appendix Sections B and C are strongly linked to preexisting works leveraging noise to regularize the discriminator, e.g., instance noise (Sønderby et al., 2017) and diffusion GANs (Wang et al., 2023) [4].
Proposition 2 is a direct consequence of the Fokker‑Planck equation (see e.g. Jordan et al., 1998).

By Proposition 2, the convergence results (minimization of the KL and Theorem 1) are direct consequences of the fact that the studied dynamics is equivalent to the well‑known Langevin dynamics; cf. Jordan et al. (1998) and the extensive literature on this topic.

In the abstract and later in the paper, the authors state that DiffFlow describes "the learning dynamics of both SDMs and GANs"; this is incorrect since it does not describe the learning dynamics of SDMs, instead it describes their generation process.
It is not clear how Remark 1 makes the convergence result of Theorem 1 directly applicable to the general DiffFlow equation.

The organization of the paper is difficult to follow as some of the main contributions listed in the introduction are relegated to the appendix; all contributions should clearly appear in the main paper and the appendix should be in the same file.

The authors state in Section 2.2 that "the training dynamics of GANs are unstable due to the high non‑convexity of the generator and discriminator"; explaining instabilities in the training dynamics of GANs remains an open problem, so this statement should be supported with a reference.
It is not clear how the drift term $f$ can be assimilated to regularization / weight decay.
It seems that the first two equations of p. 7 are the same.
subsubsection 3.3.1 should not exist as it is the only one of its subsection.
All equations should be numbered.
The acronym SLCD is not explained in the main paper.
The paper Song et al., marked as 2020b in the paper, was actually published in 2021.
The name diffusion GANs is already taken by Wang et al. (2023) [4].
Post‑rebuttal: No part of the introduced framework provides fast sampling, as the generator is left out of the discussion.

Post‑rebuttal: The paper assimilates the inference of a GAN (pushforward generator) with its training dynamics; this assimilation is misleading and leads to an incorrect interpretation of TPDM as following a single inference dynamics.

Post‑rebuttal: The link with GANs remains incomplete both in the main paper and in the appendix; the authors should precisely describe this link in the main paper instead of relying on an incomplete discussion in the appendix.
Post‑rebuttal: The paper relies too much on its appendix; the main paper should be more self‑contained.

Post‑rebuttal: The claim on Langevin convergence is contested; the presented result is a straightforward application of existing literature on Langevin sampling (e.g., Proposition 1 by Durmus & Mouline (2018)).
Post‑rebuttal: The smoothing of the data distribution to ensure convergence already existed in the first iterations of score‑based diffusion models.
Post‑rebuttal: It is still unclear how the convergence results can be easily extended to more general dynamics; the added comment in the revision should be more explicit.
Even though the overall formulation of DiffFlow is clear, the reasoning of why such formulation is useful is not comprehensive.
The presentation about the diffusion‑GAN algorithm and convergence analysis of DiffFlow is not well structured.

Many insightful discussions about the training of GANs, pseudocode of the actual algorithm, further theoretical results, etc., are deferred to the appendix, making readers question the real contribution of the proposed algorithm and theory.
Lack of experiments: the paper does not provide empirical verification on the performance of DiffFlow‑GAN.
It failed to show experimental results; confirmation was needed through experimental results if the proposed DiffFlow model truly integrates GANs and SDMs.

The instantiation to GANs is given via a coarse approximation based on the density ratio, which is not as direct; some popular GAN methods (e.g., IPM‑based GANs such as Wasserstein GAN) do not admit a density‑ratio perspective.
Convergence rates are not given and only an asymptotic guarantee is provided.
There are no experimental studies on more novel or unique choices of weighting parameters.
